bad_rate_by_vintage.png: The 12-month bad rate (navy) is measured on every loan over the same one-year window, so vintages are comparable. The old lifetime resolved-only label (orange) is distorted where many loans were still open at the data cut (right panel).
vintage_curves.png: Each line is a year of lending. Newer vintages default faster and higher. 2016 is only fully observable for roughly two years, so its curve stops early.
missingness.png: Most blanks are 'never happened' cases (no delinquency, no public record). We keep them as their own category rather than guessing a value.
iv_bar.png: Longer bar = better at separating good from bad borrowers. FICO and utilisation-type variables lead; nothing exceeds 0.5, so no variable looks like leakage.
woe_bins_top6.png: Bars are the bad rate in each band, the orange line is its WoE. Bands are monotone: as the variable moves, risk moves one way only.
corr_heatmap.png: Red/blue squares mark features that move together. After pruning, no pair exceeds 0.7, so each variable adds distinct information.
vif_bar.png: VIF measures how well other inputs can predict a given input. Everything is under the red line (5), so coefficients will be stable.
odds_ratio_forest.png: Right of the red line = raises the odds of default, left = lowers them. Intervals that avoid the line are statistically clear effects.
ladder_coefficients.png: Plain coefficients are the largest; ridge shrinks them, lasso and ElasticNet push weak ones to exactly zero. Strong drivers keep their sign on every rung.
imbalance_comparison.png: Rebalancing does not improve ranking (AUC) but it distorts the probabilities (worse Brier). A PD model needs well-calibrated probabilities, so we keep the natural class mix.
coef_stability.png: Tiny whiskers mean the coefficient barely moves when the training data is reshuffled, which is what a stable model looks like.
calibration_scorecard_valid.png: Points on the dashed line mean predicted risk equals actual risk. Calibration was fitted on validation, so this is an in-sample check; the real test is OOT.
shap_beeswarm.png: Each dot is a borrower. Right = pushes predicted default risk up, left = down; red = high value of the feature. Higher FICO (red) sits on the left, as it should.
shap_waterfall.png: How one applicant's risk is built up: each bar is a feature pushing the log-odds of default up (red) or down (blue) from the average borrower. These become the reason codes.
roc_pr_oot.png: ROC: further toward the top-left is better. Models are close to each other; the dashed purple line uses LendingClub's own grade as an input and shows how much of the gap is just LC's risk model.
ks_curve.png: KS is the widest vertical gap between the share of bad and good borrowers caught at a threshold. A bigger gap means better separation.
reliability_oot.png: Points on the dashed line mean predicted PD equals the observed 2016 bad rate; above it the model under-predicted risk, below it over-predicted. Calibration was fitted on validation only.
lift_gains.png: The riskiest 10% of applicants default at a multiple of the average rate, and the riskiest 30% contain a disproportionate share of all bad loans.
score_distribution.png: Good borrowers (blue) sit to the right of bad borrowers (red) but the two overlap a lot, which is normal for unsecured consumer credit and explains a Gini well below 0.8.
psi_bar.png: Bars show how far each input's distribution moved between the training years and 2016. Under 0.10 is stable; over 0.25 would trigger investigation.
drift_by_quarter.png: Predicted versus actual 12-month bad rate by issue quarter. Calibration was fitted on 2015H2 only; the 2016 quarters are out of time.
grade_pd_vs_actual.png: Blue is what each grade promised (validation), red is what happened in 2016. Grades should be ordered; gaps between the bars show where recalibration would be triggered.
cutoff_profit.png: Approving everyone is not best; profit peaks where the next-riskiest borrowers cost more in expected loss than they earn. The peak depends heavily on the assumed margin and LGD (see sensitivity table).
calibration_longrun.png: Red is what happened in 2016. Navy is the calibration fitted on four validation months, teal is the long-run (2013-2015) anchored version with a stated safety margin. 2016 was a worse year than the long-run average, so the through-the-cycle PD sits below it.
chargeoff_lastpay_month.png: Blue bars are charged-off loans whose last payment fell by month 9 and are labelled bad; grey bars stopped paying later and count as good inside the 12-month window.
rolling_origin.png: Each pair of bars is a model trained only on earlier years and tested on the next year. Similar heights mean the ranking power is stable; the right panel shows whether the calibration drifts as the economy changes.
realised_economics.png: Left: profit per application against the cut-off using assumed economics (grey) and what was actually collected (colours). Right: realised net return by risk grade. Realised cash is lifetime-to-date and before funding cost, so levels are not comparable to the 12-month assumption, but the shape shows where the riskiest grades stop paying for themselves.
cap_curve.png: The further a curve bows above the dashed diagonal, the better the model concentrates bad loans at the top of its risk ranking. The accuracy ratio (AR) summarises the area and equals the Gini for a yes/no outcome.
fairness_income.png: Left: share of applicants approved in each income band at the cut-off, with the four-fifths screen line. Right: predicted vs observed default rate per band; similar bars mean the model is not systematically over- or under-rating a band.
reject_vs_accepted.png: Left and middle: accepted applications (blue) against rejected ones (red); rejects ask for similar amounts but carry higher DTI. Right: the share of applications accepted falls as DTI rises. Risk_Score is not plotted because it is blank for most rejects after 2014.
pdp_ale_top_features.png: How the boosted model's predicted risk moves as one input changes, other inputs held as observed. Rising curves mean risk goes up with the feature. Constrained features are flat or one-directional by construction; the others are checked against business expectation.
